svg.title: String.split vs fixed-width fields: fixed width
svg.desc: The same decoder cuts the same two records at the offsets their layout fixes: the name in columns 0 to 11, then the two airports, the flight, and the seat. Five substring calls return the same five fields as split, and only the name needs strip() for its padding. No call compiles a Pattern or searches the record for spaces, and the second record, whose name is shorter, is cut at the same offsets.
svg.text: Fixed width: cut each field at its offset
The layout fixes where every field starts and ends, so decode() cuts each one with substring.

g.text: The layout fixes every field: the name always spans columns 0 to 11, the seat 28 to 31.
decode() cuts each field at its offset with substring. Only the name needs strip() for its padding.
Five substring calls give the five fields. decode() builds no Pattern or Matcher and never searches the record for spaces.
The next record has a shorter name and more padding, but every field starts at the same offset.
The same fields as split("\\s+") on both records, and decode() compiled no regex on either call.

svg.text: Sources: the Java SE 25 API for String, and the JDK 25 source of String.split (its fast path and Pattern.compile).
